newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil gov't "certain" of re-election victory-whip.
newsitem.headline: Brazil gov't "certain" of re-election victory-whip.

text.p: The Brazilian government is not just confident, it is certain it has enough support to win a first vote on a bill allowing President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to run for a second term, a senior whip said.

"We're not talking about confidence any more, the word is certainty," Dep. Inocencio Oliveira, lower house leader of the government-allied Liberal Front Party (PFL), said after Cardoso met with his whips to discuss the re-election vote.

The government intends to hold a first of two votes on a constitutional amendment allowing re-election on either Tuesday or Wednesday and needs a three-fifths majority, equivalent to 308 votes, on each occasion for its approval.
The bill would then move on to the Senate.

Oliveira said the government expected between 340 and 350 deputies to vote in favor of the amendment, including 60 members of the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) whose members have been divided on whether or not to vote for re-election.
But members of the PMDB's anti-government wing challenged Oliveira's upbeat prediction.
"At least half the PMDB's lawmakers won't show up for the vote," the party's president Dep. Antonio Paes de Andrade, a leading anti-re-electionist, told local newswire Invest News.
The PMDB is Brazil's biggest party with 102 members of a total 513 members of the Chamber of Deputies and is crucial to the government's chances of getting re-election approved.

Paes de Andrade was due to meet later in Rio de Janeiro with former president Itamar Franco who is being groomed by the anti-Cardoso group within the PMDB as a possible presidential candidate in 1998.

Cardoso originally hoped to put re-election to both its lower house votes during a special session of Congress called to run through the January recess, opening the way for progress on pension, civil service and tax reforms which have been paralysed.
That plan was knocked off course by senior PMDB leaders who insisted elections to run the Chamber of Deputies and Senate had to come first.

Cardoso spent last week meeting with deputies from the PMDB and other parties in a bid to muster the necessary support for the re-election bill and seemed to have clinched the support of powerful PMDB senator and former president Jose Sarney.
If the re-election is approved this week the government hopes to hold a second lower house vote on the bill after Carnival, around February 15.
